lessons.title: Constructing the Volatility Surface from the NSE Options Chain

children.text: A new quant analyst pulls up the Nifty options chain, inverts Black-Scholes on the at-the-money call, gets 13.2%, and writes 'Nifty IV is 13.2%' in a note to the desk. The desk head sends it back. There is no such thing as a single IV for Nifty on a given day. There is an IV for every strike, at every expiry, and those numbers are almost never the same. This lesson builds the full picture, the volatility surface, out of the single-option machinery from the last lesson.

body.text: Implied volatility is not one number. It is a function of strike and time to expiry, IV(K, T). Invert Black-Scholes at every liquid strike and every listed expiry on the NSE chain, and you get a grid of numbers called the volatility surface.

children.text: From One IV to a Curve

markDefs.definition: How far a strike sits from the current spot price, usually expressed as strike divided by spot, or as a percentage distance. Strikes below spot are OTM for puts and ITM for calls; strikes above spot are OTM for calls and ITM for puts.

children.text: Fix one expiry, say 30 days out, and run the implied-volatility solver from the last lesson at every strike NSE lists for that expiry. Plot the resulting IV against strike, or against

, and you rarely get a flat line. Nifty and Bank Nifty almost always show a curve that dips near the at-the-money strike and rises on both wings, and rises faster on the downside wing than the upside wing. This shape is called a smile when roughly symmetric and a smirk or skew when lopsided, and Nifty is reliably the second kind. Chapter 2 explains why. For now, treat it as an observed fact you need to be able to reconstruct on demand.

body.caption: Illustrative Nifty IV smile, single 30-day expiry, spot at 26,500 (representative shape, not live data)

body.title: Illustrative Nifty IV smile at one 30-day expiry

body.text: Look at strikes equidistant from spot: 25,700 is 800 points below, 27,300 is 800 points above. The put-side strike prices in 16.8% while the equivalent call-side strike prices in only 14.9%. That asymmetry, higher IV on the downside, is the skew this course is named after. It is not noise. It is the market charging more to insure against a crash than to insure against a melt-up, and Chapter 2 puts a precise number on exactly how much more.

children.text: Extend the single-strike solver from the last lesson into a loop over the chain. The structure below pulls a strike, its option type and its mid price for each leg, and returns the IV at every strike. The mid prices here are illustrative placeholders, in a live system this list comes straight from the NSE options chain feed.

body.code:
from scipy.optimize import brentq
from scipy.stats import norm
import numpy as np

def bs_price(S, K, T, r, sigma, option_type):
    d1 = (np.log(S / K) + (r + 0.5 * sigma ** 2) * T) / (sigma * np.sqrt(T))
    d2 = d1 - sigma * np.sqrt(T)
    if option_type == "call":
        return S * norm.cdf(d1) - K * np.exp(-r * T) * norm.cdf(d2)
    return K * np.exp(-r * T) * norm.cdf(-d2) - S * norm.cdf(-d1)

def implied_vol(mid_price, S, K, T, r, option_type):
    objective = lambda sigma: bs_price(S, K, T, r, sigma, option_type) - mid_price
    return brentq(objective, 1e-4, 5.0)

# Illustrative chain, one 30-day expiry, spot = 26,500
# Convention: use OTM legs only, puts below spot, calls above spot
chain = [
    {"strike": 25700, "type": "put",  "mid": 96.40},
    {"strike": 25900, "type": "put",  "mid": 128.75},
    {"strike": 26100, "type": "put",  "mid": 168.90},
    {"strike": 26300, "type": "put",  "mid": 218.55},
    {"strike": 26700, "type": "call", "mid": 228.30},
    {"strike": 26900, "type": "call", "mid": 165.10},
    {"strike": 27100, "type": "call", "mid": 117.85},
    {"strike": 27300, "type": "call", "mid": 83.20},
]

S, T, r = 26500, 30 / 365, 0.065

smile = [
    (leg["strike"], round(implied_vol(leg["mid"], S, leg["strike"], T, r, leg["type"]) * 100, 2))
    for leg in chain
]
print(smile)
body.caption: Looping the single-strike IV solver across an options chain to build the smile. Run it to see the IV at each strike, rather than trusting a hardcoded table.

children.text: Why OTM Legs, and Put-Call Parity

Notice the chain above uses puts below spot and calls above spot, never the reverse. In-the-money options trade wider, have lower volume, and their price is dominated by intrinsic value, so a small bid-ask bounce swings the solved IV by a large, noisy amount. Out-of-the-money options are pure time value, more liquid on NSE, and give a cleaner IV read. If you need the ITM-side view of the same strike anyway, for instance to sanity-check a quote, you get there through put-call parity instead of solving the illiquid ITM leg directly.

body.caption: Put-call parity for European options on a non-dividend-paying underlying, ignoring the small index dividend-yield adjustment desks apply in practice

body.title: Reading the put price off parity
body.prompt: Using put-call parity, C − P = S − K·e^(−rT). For the 26,500 strike, 30-day Nifty expiry from the last lesson: S = 26,500, K = 26,500, r = 6.5%, T = 30/365, and the call trades at ₹385.00. What is the parity-implied put price, in rupees, to one decimal place?
body.explanation: K·e^(−rT) = 26,500 × e^(−0.065 × 30/365) ≈ 26,500 × 0.99467 ≈ 26,358.8. So S − K·e^(−rT) ≈ 26,500 − 26,358.8 = 141.2. Rearranging parity, P = C − (S − K·e^(−rT)) = 385.0 − 141.2 = ₹243.8. This is exactly why a desk can quote a reliable OTM put price, or sanity-check one, even when the ITM call at the same strike is barely traded, at the same implied volatility parity assumes holds for both legs.

body.title: Which leg to solve
body.question: You need the implied volatility at the 25,900 strike for a Nifty expiry, with spot at 26,500. Which price should you invert Black-Scholes on?
options: The 25,900 call, because calls are always more liquid
The 25,900 put, because it is out-of-the-money and typically has a tighter, more informative market
Whichever of the call or put last traded, regardless of moneyness
The average of the call and put prices at that strike
body.explanation: 25,900 is below the 26,500 spot, so the put at that strike is out-of-the-money and the call is in-the-money. OTM options carry pure time value and tighter markets on index chains, making their quoted price a cleaner input for the IV solver. The ITM call at the same strike should, under put-call parity, imply the same volatility, but its own quote is noisier and not the one you solve directly.

children.text: Repeat the whole exercise for every expiry NSE lists on the underlying, weekly and monthly Nifty and Bank Nifty contracts out to several months, and you get one smile per expiry. Stack them and you have moved from a curve to a surface: IV as a function of both strike and time to expiry. Near-dated and far-dated smiles are rarely identical in shape or level, which is the subject of Chapter 3.

body.title: Illustrative smile shape across two expiries (representative pattern, not live data)

body.text: The near-dated smile is steeper on both wings than the far-dated one. A weekly expiry has less time for the underlying to drift back toward the strike if it moves sharply, so a given percentage move matters more, and the market prices the tails more aggressively. As expiry stretches out, moves have more time to mean-revert or offset, and the smile typically flattens. This is a preview, not the full explanation, Chapter 3 builds the term structure formally.

body.label: NSE strike spacing is not fixed
body.value: Strike intervals scale with the index level and are set out in NSE circulars, not a single constant
body.context: Older, lower-index-level Nifty chains commonly used 50-point intervals near the money. As the index level has risen, NSE has periodically widened strike intervals in its contract specifications. Always pull the current strike list for the specific expiry from the live NSE chain rather than assuming a fixed spacing when building a surface programmatically.

body.title: What if the chain has a break: a strike that doesn't fit the curve

children.text: Real chains are messier than a textbook curve. One strike in the middle of an otherwise smooth smile occasionally solves to an IV well above or below its neighbours. Before treating that as a genuine feature, check three things.
Is the last-traded price recent, or is it a print from earlier in the day at a different spot level?
A wide market on a thinly traded strike can put the mid price, and therefore the solved IV, almost anywhere within a broad range.
A strike with negligible open interest is easy to mismark and hard to trade out of, so its IV carries little information.

Production systems typically use the tighter, more liquid quote when both are available, apply outlier filters against neighbouring strikes, and interpolate across a bad point rather than feeding it into a pricing model as-is.

body.title: The strike that doesn't fit
body.scenario: You are rebuilding the 30-day Nifty smile intraday. Every strike solves to an IV within a tight, smooth band except 26,100, which prints at 22.4%, well above both its neighbours at roughly 14.6%. Checking the terminal, the 26,100 put last traded four hours ago, the current bid-ask on it is ₹142 to ₹198, and its open interest is a fraction of the neighbouring strikes.
body.prompt: What do you do with this data point before it feeds into the rest of your surface-construction pipeline?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Treat 22.4% as suspect, not as a genuine kink in the smile. A single-strike spike surrounded by smooth neighbours is far more often bad data than a real market signal.
2. The evidence supports that: a four-hour-old last-traded price, a wide ₹142 to ₹198 market, and thin open interest all point to a stale, unreliable quote rather than fresh information.
3. Re-price using the current mid of the live bid-ask, ₹170, instead of the stale last-traded price, and re-solve the IV from that.
4. If the recomputed IV still looks out of line with neighbouring strikes, exclude that point from the surface and interpolate it from the surrounding strikes instead of feeding a noisy number into downstream Greeks or pricing.
5. Log the exclusion. A surface-construction pipeline that silently drops or overrides data points without a record becomes impossible to debug when a real dislocation does happen and needs to be trusted.

cards.definition: Implied volatility expressed as a function of both strike and time to expiry, IV(K, T), built by solving for IV at every liquid strike and expiry on the chain.
The shape of IV plotted against strike for a single expiry. Roughly symmetric is a smile; skewed toward one wing, as on Nifty, is a smirk.
A strike's position relative to spot, commonly K/S, used to compare smiles across different spot levels or underlyings on a common x-axis.
C − P = S − K·e^(−rT). Links call and put prices at the same strike and expiry, letting you derive a reliable price for an illiquid leg from a liquid one.
The market practice of solving implied volatility from out-of-the-money option prices, since they are more liquid and carry pure time value, rather than from noisier in-the-money quotes.

points: Implied volatility is a function of strike and expiry, IV(K, T), not a single number. Solving it at every liquid strike for one expiry gives a smile; repeating across expiries builds the full surface.
Nifty's smile is typically a skewed smirk, with OTM puts pricing higher IV than equidistant OTM calls, foreshadowing the skew mechanics covered in Chapter 2.
Build the smile from out-of-the-money option prices, puts below spot and calls above spot, since they are more liquid and cleaner to invert than in-the-money quotes.
Put-call parity, C − P = S − K·e^(−rT), lets you derive or sanity-check a price on one leg from the other at the same strike, without needing to solve the noisier leg directly.
Near-dated smiles are usually steeper than far-dated ones, a first look at the term structure formalized in Chapter 3.
Treat outlier strikes as suspect data first: check staleness, bid-ask width and open interest before accepting a kink as a genuine feature of the surface.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment or trading advice. The option chain, prices and IV figures used here are illustrative teaching data, not live NSE quotes, unless explicitly stated otherwise. NSE strike intervals and contract specifications change over time; always confirm current specifications from NSE's own circulars before building production systems. Consult a SEBI-registered adviser before trading.
